“Fine, then you can take the beach for yourself, you selfish brat!” the man in front of him yelled, then grabbed a handful of sand and chucked it straight into Mydei’s face.

“You! What even—” He rubbed the sand from his eyes, then glared back at the man in front of him. “I said I don’t want any problems! I just told you and your friends there to take your trash and not leave it on the beach! You see that?” He pointed at the sign that said ‘Don’t throw rubbish on the beach’.

“Pick up your trash!” Mydei yelled.

But the man just glared at him, his expression shifting with pride.

“Let’s just go, guys. The rumors were right — this beach really is guarded by some ruthless prick,” he said, and his friends nodded, of course not forgetting to throw more sand at him before leaving.

Mydei glared after them, watching as they walked away from the beach.

He sighed as the beach fell silent again. It was always the same every day. He tried to keep the beach clean, but every time visitors came, they just ended up trashing it all over again. 

Once, he tried to warn a family having a picnic on the beach not to throw their trash on the sand, only for the mother to go full Karen on him, yelling that the trash would end up in the sea anyway before demanding to speak to some manager who didn’t even exist.

Then there was the college frat crowd having a barbecue on the sand. They were loud, the kind of crowd Mydei didn’t like. They played music too loud and tossed chip bags and bottles everywhere.

When Mydei tried to warn them, someone poured soda over his head and laughed in his face, calling him lame. That made his anger boil over, and before he knew it, he was already in a fistfight.

Both sides ended up bruised, and the fight kept going until someone called the cops. When the police arrived, they were all taken to the station for questioning. 

Mydei explained what happened, and at least this time, the police were on his side. They agreed with him about the mess people kept making of the beach.

Maybe that was where all the “scary beach guard” stories started — because after that, the number of visitors coming to the beach grew lower and lower, until eventually, no one came at all.

Days turned quiet after that. The beach stayed empty, the air still, filled only with the sound of the waves. But Mydei still came every morning, cleaning what little trash the wind carried in, fixing the broken signs, and watching the sun rise and set every day.

He lived just a short walk away, in a small house he’d bought with what little he’d earned working as a chef before. It was more of a shack than a home, the roof leaked when it rained, and the walls creaked when the wind blew, but it was close to the sea, and that was enough for him.

It had been about two years since he moved to where he lived now, after his mother passed away. The old house they’d shared felt too quiet without her. Every corner reminded him of what he’d lost, so he left, hoping to find his own peace somewhere far away.

Mydei came here and chose this place, of all places, hoping the beach and the sound of the waves might drown out the loneliness. He hoped he could find some peace again, or at least something that felt close to it.

The waves and the salty air were enchanting, and even the squall of seagulls overhead felt like part of the magic. The beach near his home had white sand and clear water, and that was why he wanted to keep it clean. It was already beautiful as it was.

He liked imagining the beach was his alone to explore. There were tall rocks where he fished every day, but he never stayed in one place for long, always moving around to see more. It felt like a special place where he could keep discovering something new.

All the elements seemed to come together here, the water of the waves, the fire of the sun blazing in the sky, the earth of the sand beneath his feet, and the air of the warm breeze against his skin.

There was one place he liked to visit that felt especially magical. It was a bit of a hike to reach, winding around towering sea stacks and climbing over jagged boulders, but it was always worth the cuts and scrapes it took to get there.

Mydei could sit right in the middle of it, surrounded by rocks that curved around him like a crescent moon, shutting out the rest of the beach.

It was the perfect place to watch the sun rise and fall over the horizon, a quiet spot where peace felt real. His own small paradise, beautiful and untouched, the only place that ever felt like home.

Even after the sun set, he could bring a book there and read under the soft glow of the moonlight until midnight. Sometimes, he’d bring a blanket and fall asleep right there, surrounded by the sound of the waves and the whisper of the wind, waking at dawn to watch the sunrise.

Mydei’s morning walks now always included carrying a trash bag with him, picking up litter no matter how small. He needed to keep the beach clean because it was part of his home too.

He sometimes wished he could make the rude tourists leave and never come back, but there wasn’t much he could do since it was a public beach. He even thought once about reporting a fake shark sighting, hoping it would scare them off, but it didn’t feel right to blame the poor sharks for something they didn’t do. 

So, in the end, he was fine being called the ruthless beach guard or whatever they wanted to call him, as long as they didn’t come back and trash his beach anymore.

Mydei was walking along the beach that morning, picking up trash as always, when he noticed something glimmering in the distance under the sun. Assuming it was just another piece of litter, he walked toward it and knelt in the sand to pick it up so he could throw it away.

To his surprise, it wasn’t trash at all. It was a piece of sea glass, rounded and smooth from being polished by the waves. It shone a deep, vivid red, bright enough to almost glow in his hand.

It looked like it had been washed ashore by the tide, but something about it made him think otherwise. Its placement seemed intentional, almost like an offering, resting neatly on a small flat rock as if someone had put it there on purpose. He wondered for a moment if that was the case.

Maybe it was placed there on purpose, maybe not — either way, it was Mydei’s now.

He loved sea glass, though he had never been very good at finding it. He had one piece, a jagged blue one, that he had turned into an ornament. He wrapped it with wire and hung it by the window alongside small trinkets that clinked softly whenever the wind blew through.

This red piece was much bigger, and its color was brilliant. He was thrilled to have found it and was already thinking about what he could make with such a beautiful prize. Maybe a necklace. Or a bracelet, perhaps.

“Thank you,” Mydei said out loud to the sea. “I mean, thanks for holding on to it for a while until it got this nice shape. It’s not like you walked up here and placed it on this little rock for me. Heh. But I appreciate it.”

There was no reply, of course, except for the steady crash of the waves. But Mydei liked to think it was the sea saying you’re welcome.

Mydei tucked the sea glass into his pocket and continued checking the rest of the beach for trash. He found a few beer cans, cigarette butts, and pieces of broken styrofoam. He couldn’t explain it, but as he worked, he had an odd feeling that someone was watching him.

It was silly. He knew there was no one else out here. And yet…

Mydei swore there were eyes on him.

He looked around to make sure that wasn’t the case, and when he finally felt the beach was clean enough, he headed home and didn’t think much more about it.

The next day, Mydei found another treasure waiting for him on the rock — more sea glass. This time, it was two matching pieces, a deep blue so dark it was almost black.

The day after that, there was another piece, a slightly different shade of red, like the first one he’d found.

Then came purple, green, yellow, and every different color.

By the end of the week, Mydei had gathered enough sea glass to make necklaces and bracelets.

He was starting to get suspicious. There was no way the tide could have brought all of it in like that.

No. Someone had to be leaving these pieces on the sand. But why? And who? Were they actually meant for him?

Other than the occasional visitors who littered everywhere, Mydei never really saw anyone else around. It almost felt like someone was leaving these treasures specifically for him to find, though he had no real reason to believe that. Still, he felt grateful — whether they were meant for him or not, he loved the treasures.

So he decided to test it, to see if the treasures were really meant for him. For the next few days, he changed his routine, sometimes arriving earlier, sometimes later, and even skipping a day just to see what would happen. He let the visitors come and go, only stepping in if they got too careless with their trash.

Each time he returned, no matter the hour or the day, there was always a new treasure waiting in the same spot.

It felt too precise to be a coincidence. It was as if someone knew exactly when he would come.

Which meant someone really was watching him.

Mydei had suspected it for a while. Whenever he walked along the beach, the hairs on the back of his neck would stand up, as if sensing that he wasn’t alone, a feeling he couldn’t quite shake. 

Yet, even though it felt strange, he wasn’t afraid. Whoever it was didn’t seem to mean him any harm. Mydei’s routine wasn’t hard to figure out, since he came to the beach nearly every morning. If someone wanted to do something bad, they would have had plenty of chances by now.

He told himself that whoever this person was could have acted a long time ago but never did, though that didn’t make the situation any less unsettling.

Still, the gifts kept appearing on the shore, always placed on the same rock. Most of the time it was sea glass, but sometimes there were seashells or polished stones. Once, there was even an old gold coin that looked centuries old.

One day, after watching the sunset, Mydei left a ring on the same rock where he always found his gifts. The ring had once belonged to his mother, and ever since she passed, he had kept it with him. His mysterious gifter had given him so many lovely things, so it felt right to give something back — even if it was the one thing he never thought he could part with. But for this mysterious giver, he was willing to try.
      
The next morning when Mydei visited, the ring was gone, and in its place was a gorgeous pearl bracelet. He stared at it, wide-eyed, the sunlight glinting off each smooth bead. This time, he was sure of it. There was no way this was a coincidence.

That night, he decided he was going to find out who was behind it. Mydei packed his sleeping bag, some snacks, and a few drinks, then snuck out in the evening as soon as the sun went down.

His plan was simple. He would wait for his mysterious gifter to show up and make the exchange.
